summary: Research a car and EV-battery diagnostic center (full-body scanner plus vehicle data, reports sold to service centers) with a skeptic pass and a verdict on fit with our battery take-back business

findings.angle: A: Existing drive-through / "full body" vehicle scanners and AI inspection systems, and whether anything inspects an installed EV battery pack (research date 31 Oct 2026)
findings.summary: Drive-through vehicle scanners are real and commercial. UVeye is the clear leader (vendor claims 1,200+ systems, 4M+ vehicles per month). They are cheap per scan but cost EUR 150-250k to buy (German examples) or about USD 3-6k per month on subscription (low-confidence US estimates). What they see is the car's skin, tyres and the underside: dents and scratches, tyre tread and pressure, leaks, rust, missing parts, bent or damaged components. For an installed EV battery they can at best show the pack's outer casing (dents, punctures, deformation, leaks, mounting problems). I found no evidence that any camera drive-through scanner measures battery state of health, capacity, cell balance or internal faults. UVeye's CEO talked about battery sensors in 2023, and a 2025 trade article says thermal imaging for EV battery monitoring is "being integrated", but I found no shipped product and no independent accuracy data. A smaller vendor (Vumo) implies a battery-condition estimate, but its own product page does not mention EV batteries. The few technologies that look inside an installed pack are X-ray / CT (Fraunhofer XXL-CT, the AIR full-vehicle radiography system). These show mechanical integrity (displacement, deformation, swelling), not capacity, and are research or lab facilities, far too expensive and slow for a service-centre lane. Real SoH numbers come from reading the BMS or measuring through the OBD port (DEKRA about 15 min; Aviloo Flash about 3 min, GBP 35 dealer cost, EUR 79 at ADAC Schleswig-Holstein) - that is the layer where our business lives. Practical conclusion: a scanner lane is a sensible "intake and underbody" tool that can flag battery-casing damage, but it does not replace an SoH test. It would be a cheap add-on feeding our triage, not the diagnosis itself. In Europe, deployments are thin: UVeye's European footprint is mostly Amazon fleet sites plus a new UK/EU team; Mercedes has about 40 camera scanners at German dealers; TÜV SÜD's DVS is a "handful" in Germany. I found no Baltic or Latvian deployment and no CSDD automated scanning lane. All pricing from vendors is quote-only; every figure below carries its source type and date. Several useful numbers (UVeye valuation, subscription prices, Proov lease) are third-party or undated and flagged as such.

items.topic: Thermal imaging of installed EV batteries - what it can and cannot do
items.finding: Infrared cameras read surface temperature only and cannot see through glass or the sealed pack housing; they need an active load and a baseline under controlled conditions to be meaningful. Heat patterns can hint at hot spots or faults but do not give capacity/SoH (80% SoH is a capacity criterion). In research, thermography is combined with ultrasound and X-ray CT rather than used alone (Birmingham 2026 paper). In a static drive-through at ambient temperature a parked car's pack is thermally quiet, so a drive-through thermal image mainly shows whatever heat the car happens to emit (my inference). Thermal cameras cost 5-10x general cameras per a patent (cost remark only).

items.topic: X-ray / CT of installed EV batteries and security vehicle scanners
items.finding: Fraunhofer IIS XXL-CT can scan complete battery modules/packs while installed in a car, nondestructively; resolution 0.5-1 mm for installed modules (about 0.1 mm for small compact modules); industrial customers must come to Furth; vehicle must be upright; method 'too expensive for private individuals'; gantry CT for natural-position scanning is still a development goal (interview 31 Jan 2023). AIR (Fraunhofer + Hochschule Munchen): 2D X-ray, 360 kV source, 'radiation-safe scanning of entire vehicles'; detects layer misalignment, local deformation and swelling; focus is mechanical integrity, NOT state of health; images reviewed manually (ASNT Materials Evaluation, May 2026). Search summary reports about 5 minutes per pack in test environment (unverified). Security scanners (Smiths Detection HCVP/HCVM, Rapiscan Eagle/C10) are customs/border drive-through X-ray for contraband; no list prices published; US CBP contracts only; not used for battery health. So X-ray can show a swollen or displaced cell stack, but cannot tell you 83% vs 91% SoH.

items.topic: What a drive-through scanner can and cannot say about an installed EV battery (synthesis)
items.finding: CAN (plausibly, with vendor and trade-press support but no independent validation): visible casing damage on the underside (dents, punctures, scrapes, deformation), coolant/oil/fluid leaks near the pack, missing or loose underbody shields and fasteners, corrosion, evidence of repairs or incorrect re-installation (Instavalo claim). CANNOT: capacity or SoH, internal resistance, cell imbalance, cell chemistry or manufacturer, history of fast-charging, internal short circuits, swelling hidden inside the housing, insulation resistance, software/BMS faults. Those need BMS/OBD data (DEKRA about 15 min; Aviloo Flash about 3 min) or lab/X-ray. Many EV packs are covered by under-body plates, so a camera sees the plate, not the pack. Hence a scanner is a screen for physical damage and a triage trigger, not a battery test. Marketing to treat sceptically: 'MRI for vehicles', 'estimates EV battery condition' (Vumo snippet, not on its page), 'accuracy up to 95%' (Vumo, undefined metric), '96% / 0.5 mm' (low-quality article).

items.topic: Cost summary for the service-centre scanner idea

findings.angle: B: How EV battery health is actually measured on an installed pack, who may access the data, equipment cost, and regulatory (PTI, Reg 2023/1542 Art. 14, Data Act, Reg 2018/858) state as of 31 Oct 2026
findings.summary: Installed-pack health measurement today = (1) OBD/UDS read of BMS data (SoC, cell/module voltages, temperatures, insulation, DTCs, and an OEM-defined SoH where exposed), (2) software-derived SoH from cloud models (AVILOO FLASH ~3 min, TUV NORD, TEXA, Bosch/Autel), or (3) loaded tests (DEKRA short acceleration for internal resistance ~15 min; Hella Gutmann/TWAICE Battery Quick Check load during AC charging ~1 h; AVILOO PREMIUM full-cycle drive). Only a full charge/discharge or controlled-load test gives a true capacity number; quick tests are statistical estimates. Vendor accuracy claims are +/-2.5% (DEKRA, only at 10-30C, MAE <9% over -10..40C per vendor slide) and +/-3% (AVILOO, vs its own PREMIUM, 95% of reference measurements); I found NO independent third-party validation. An independent preprint (1,114 EVs, 5 makers) found BMS-reported SoH poorly correlated with measured capacity (rho 0.10-0.62) and 384 vehicles expose no SoH at all, i.e. the BMS number itself is unreliable. A drive-through 'full body scanner' cannot see capacity: X-ray (Fraunhofer AIR, 360 kV, ~5-10 min) can show cell swelling/deformation/misalignment only, is research-stage with no price or commercial availability; ultrasonic/CT on installed packs has no field validation found; thermal imaging only sees pack-casing surface heat and is vendor-claim territory; underbody scanners (UVeye) check casing damage, pricing confidential. Regulatory: EU Roadworthiness Package (2025/0097(COD)) is still in legislative process (Council general approach 5 Dec 2025; EP TRAN 5 May 2026), EV items included but no uniform EU SoH method; Reg 2023/1542 Art. 14 requires BMS to hold SoH data from 18 Aug 2024 but who may read it ('legitimate interest') depends on implementing acts/Annex XIII and is contested; Reg 2018/858 Art. 61 gives independent operators OBD/RMI access, with Delegated Reg 2026/699 letting OEMs apply certificate/token security from 23 Jun 2026 and API duties phased 2026-2028; Data Act applicable since 12 Sep 2025 (vehicle design obligation from 12 Sep 2026). Implication for the idea: a scanner adds value for mechanical/underbody/thermal/DTC triage and as a data-aggregation wrapper, but the battery-health core is an OBD+cloud SoH or loaded test that others (AVILOO, TUV, DEKRA, TEXA, Hella) already sell; licensing (AVILOO partner terms, DEKRA SaaS = subscription + per-report) is the realistic route rather than building a measurement method.

items.topic: AVILOO FLASH and PREMIUM tests (OBD/cloud SoH)
items.finding: FLASH is an OBD box test taking ~3 min stationary; SoH from an ML/statistical model trained on tens/hundreds of thousands of PREMIUM and comparable tests. PREMIUM records a drive with a full-cycle style data set. AVILOO claims +/-3% deviation for FLASH vs PREMIUM and says warranty terms specify max 3% deviation in at least 95% of reference measurements. These are company statements; a critical article says no independent academic body has replicated/validated the algorithm. AVILOO itself states SoH can differ strongly by reference value and calculation method. Partner model: software licence plus boxes, licence fees in an order form (not public); no per-test price for garages found. Consumer-side historic price: TUV SUD offered AVILOO box+certificate for EUR 99 (EUR 49 certificate-only launch offer), April 2022. Aggregate fleet data: 500,000+ FLASH tests, 20 models, spread between individual cars of the same model can exceed 12 percentage points at 150,000 km (Ioniq 5), medians mostly 80-93% at 150,000 km.

items.topic: DEKRA battery quick test (short load, internal resistance)
items.finding: DEKRA's method reads static data via OBD dongle (current, voltage, cell temp, cell voltages, SoC), then a ~100 m short, steady acceleration records current/voltage to compute internal resistance, mapped to SoH against type-specific reference data from test drives. DEKRA states max average error +/-2.5% only under defined boundary conditions (10-30C); validated by RWTH Aachen with MAE below 9% SoH across -10 to 40C. Result in ~15 minutes via web app; patent WO 2021/099102 A1. Business models: DEKRA experts performing it, or SaaS (authorised trained personnel; subscription + price per report; API to customer system). DEKRA slide itself says today manufacturer data cannot be read out consistently to get SoH and that the only alternative is a full charge/discharge (time-consuming). Price not stated. Note this is an impedance-based proxy for capacity, i.e. a statistical mapping, validated by the vendor/university, not an independent lab-capacity comparison I could review.

items.topic: Accuracy evidence: SoH tests vs lab capacity
items.finding: No peer-reviewed head-to-head of a commercial OBD SoH tool vs lab capacity test was found. The only independent large dataset found (arXiv 2603.21592, submitted 23 Mar 2026 to Nature Energy, preprint, not peer reviewed) reports BMS-reported SoH does not track measured capacity: 1,114 EVs from five manufacturers over 375 days, real capacity differences of 12-25% within every model not captured by BMS SoH, correlation rho 0.10 to 0.62, 384 vehicles expose no SoH, and an independent electrochemical marker classifies degradation with 74-89% accuracy; lab cell study showed partial-voltage-window charge measurements tracking reference capacity with rho >0.80. Implication: an inspection that only reads the BMS SoH number is not trustworthy; a measured (loaded or charge-window) method is needed, and vendor accuracy claims have not been independently checked. UNECE GTR 22 (adopted 9 Mar 2022) will require SOCE (state of certified energy) monitors accessible via OBD or OTA on new BEVs, with minimum 80% SOCE for 5 y/100,000 km and 70% for 8 y/160,000 km; the monitor-accuracy statistical verification is in the GTR; this improves future comparability but does not help used cars already on the road.

items.topic: What a car 'full body scanner' can and cannot see of an installed battery (X-ray, CT, ultrasonic, thermal, underbody)
items.finding: X-ray: Fraunhofer IIS / Munich Univ. of Applied Sciences 'AIR' (Antriebsbatterieinspektion mittels Roentgentechnik) uses a 360 kV 2D X-ray source above the vehicle and detector below, scanning only the pack area; tested on >100 private EVs; shows layer misalignment, local deformation, cell swelling for prismatic/cylindrical/pouch cells; ~10 min per vehicle scan, ~5 min automated evaluation; does NOT replace electrical tests and cannot give capacity/SoH; in a crash test a VW ID.3 pack was cleared only after further hazard and electrical tests; no commercial availability, price or plan for HU use ('has not yet announced any concrete plans'); a planned 'Giant Eye' CT in Fuerth is for 3D whole-vehicle analysis. Ultrasonic: described as promising but mainly lab/production use; no installed-pack field validation found. CT: vendor claim of 50 micron resolution, no independent in-vehicle validation. Thermal imaging: vendor material says hotspots (0.3 C resolution claimed) reveal high-resistance connections or micro-shorts; an Indian service lists baseline vs under-charge scans; a camera sees only the casing/underbody surface through a pack that is shielded and liquid-cooled, so only gross anomalies would show; no standard or independent validation. Underbody scanners (UVeye, Vumo UB Scanner) detect casing damage/leaks/missing parts; UVeye pricing confidential; battery-case-crack detection is a vendor feature; one forum anecdote alleges false positive led to unneeded replacement (unverified). Water ingress and insulation faults need electrical measurement; Swiss guideline treats casing deformation >=10 mm, holes or torn casing as grounds to exclude the battery without further inspection.

items.topic: OEM access: secure gateway, Tesla, third-party tools
items.finding: Regulation (EU) 2018/858 Art. 61 + Annex X oblige OEMs to give independent operators OBD and repair/maintenance information (RMI); the Court of Justice (Scania case, 2023) held OEMs cannot add conditions beyond the regulation. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/699 (adopted 23 Mar 2026; in force 23 Jun 2026) defines which security measures (certificates, tokens, authentication of tool/maker, and for vehicle-changing access the operator/employee) OEMs may apply via secure gateways; it expands RMI on battery diagnostics, battery repair and safe handling (Annex X points 2.5.12 and 2.5.13). Phase-in: API info for non-software-update activities 23 Sep 2026; general deadline for software/web services/information to tool makers 23 Dec 2026; VIN-based packages only via API from 23 Jun 2027; software-update related 23 Jun 2028. SERMI certification (Delegated Reg 2021/1244) is required to access security-relevant RMI, certificates valid 5 years. Noerr notes the act does not settle how battery data access works in practice or the secure-gateway debate. Tesla: owner can temporarily authorise an independent workshop for remote diagnostics; Toolbox 3 (Chrome web app, 2018+ vehicles) is reported at USD 75/day, USD 150/month (cut from 500), USD 700/year, security-system actions need extra Tesla authorisation. Bosch Esitronic added Tesla and access to protected data from Ford and Porsche (press release, no date retrieved). Ford/VW/Hyundai-Kia tool prices: not searched specifically/not found.

items.topic: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 Art. 14 and Annex XIII (battery data access)
items.finding: I could not retrieve the Official Journal text (EUR-Lex fetches returned empty/429), so this relies on secondary sources and must be checked against EUR-Lex. Art. 14(1): BMS of EV, light-means-of-transport and stationary storage batteries must contain data needed to determine SoH and expected lifetime; applies from 18 Aug 2024 per EUROBAT (Dec 2025), which argues no general duty to install a BMS. Access: sources say data is available to 'persons with a legitimate interest' (repairers, refurbishers, second-life/end-of-life operators) and authorities; who counts and the scope are to be set by Commission implementing acts (Mondaq); Annex XIII restricts SoH/usage-history data to legitimate interest parties (Arianee); EUROBAT lobbies to limit access to Annex VII data for safety/IP reasons; HSF Kramer flags battery-maker competition-law concerns. Battery passport (EV batteries) applies from 18 Feb 2027 per Codibly's headline. Conclusion: the right to read SoH is real in principle but practical, standardised access (and definition of SoH) is unresolved; do not build the business on Art. 14 alone.

items.topic: EU Data Act (Reg 2023/2854) for connected vehicles
items.finding: Applicable since 12 Sep 2025; Commission issued vehicle-data guidance on 12 Sep 2025; users (and third parties they authorise, e.g. repairers) get access to connected-product data, remuneration on FRAND terms for third-party data holders; the design obligation (new connected products built for direct access) applies from 12 Sep 2026; some existing-contract obligations run to 12 Sep 2027. A Digital Omnibus proposal (COM(2025) 837) could amend connected-product rules; status unverified. Most OEMs use the 'extended vehicle' server model, so battery SoH via the Data Act depends on what the OEM lists as readily available data and on the owner's consent; the Data Act does not itself give a garage a live OBD read.

items.topic: EU Roadworthiness Package (PTI) and EV battery checks; CITA, DEKRA, TUV, CSDD
items.finding: Commission proposed the package in April 2025 (procedure 2025/0097(COD)); it foresees EV-specific periodic checks (HV battery systems, electric powertrain, integrated software). Council general approach adopted 5 Dec 2025; IRU says a uniform EU method to assess battery safety/performance at PTI is still missing. European Parliament TRAN committee adopted draft position on 5 May 2026 (30 for, 11 against, 2 abstentions): adds test items for battery-electric/hybrid vehicles, battery checks, recall check, rejects annual PTI for old cars; plenary and trilogue to follow (outcome after May 2026 not found). I found no confirmation that SoH (as capacity) will be mandatory at PTI; CITA Recommendation No. 27 (July 2025) lists 'battery health assessment', isolation resistance as a practical test and standardised access to diagnostic data, fault codes and battery software. UK-style/Directive 2014/45/EU current text does not set SoH testing. Latvia: no CSDD rule on EV battery testing found; one article says CSDD stations offer vehicle diagnostics for used-car buyers but no battery detail; carVertical Latvian help page only notes battery-wear data; no Riga SoH test price found in Latvian searches.

No implementing act is mentioned in Art. 14. The 'legitimate interest' wording belongs to the battery passport Annex XIII, not Art. 14 access. Researcher never retrieved the OJ text and the 'implementing acts decide' framing is wrong for Art. 14. Caveat: the right is for the battery owner or those acting for them (so a garage needs the owner's mandate), and practical technical access (UDS vs OEM server) is still unstandardised. corrections: Art. 14 of Reg 2023/1542 is mis-described: access is a statutory read right for whoever lawfully acquired the battery, expressly including independent economic operators, waste managers and third parties acting on their behalf (e.g. a diagnostic centre with owner mandate), 'at any time and without discrimination', for residual-value/remaining-life assessment, reuse/repurposing/remanufacturing/recycling, and energy storage. 'Legitimate interest' is the Annex XIII battery-passport concept, and no implementing act is needed for Art. 14 (para 4 is only a delegated act to amend Annex VII). This materially helps the business case; the remaining weakness is technical (no standard interface, OEM IP carve-out, SoH definition varies).

The researcher's statement that Art. 14 depends on implementing acts and 'do not build the business on Art. 14 alone' should be reframed: the legal right exists in the text; the unresolved part is practical implementation.
Roadworthiness Package status is out of date: EP plenary mandate 21 May 2026 (369/126/84) and at least two trilogues held (2nd debrief 20 Oct 2026); outcome still unknown.
360 kV is not in the electrive article (comes from the ASNT/Materials Evaluation paper); '~10 min' is an earlier Fraunhofer statement, only the ~5 min evaluation is for the new software.

Delegated Reg 2026/699 was published in the OJ on 3 Jun 2026 and the stated date 23 Jun 2026 is both entry into force and application of Appendix 4 security requirements; add the 23 Dec 2027 deadline.
Preprint caveat: fleet is Hyundai/Kia/Genesis/Audi/VW only, so it cannot be generalised to all makes; it is also unreviewed.

AVILOO fleet statistics are from AVILOO customers (self-selected) and are a vendor report distributed via trade press, not independent data; label them vendor-sourced even though electrive is trade press.

These are the only price anchors found and are commercial guides, not primary.

DEKRA SaaS model requires trained authorised personnel with compliance checks twice a year and report API integration, meaning a scanner centre would need to be a DEKRA licensee rather than build its own method.

Practical access path: owner mandate under Art. 14(2) plus Reg 2018/858 Art. 61 OBD/RMI access (with SERMI for security-relevant parts) are the two legal routes; the Data Act is a third but depends on OEM 'extended vehicle' servers.

findings.angle: C: Business models for diagnostics sold to service centers/garages (remote/outsourced diagnostics, inspection-as-a-service, battery-health B2B, report pricing, comparable companies, lessons, Latvian/Baltic price levels)
findings.summary: Research on 31 Oct 2026, from about 22 searches and 14 fetches. Several fetches failed (RDN timeouts, BCA and Auto24 403). Garages do pay for outsourced diagnostics, but the models that scale are narrow and priced low per transaction. (1) US asTech/Repairify sells a remote OEM scan as a service, tied to insurer-reimbursed collision work. It reported 12.4M scans and 28,000 customers in 2021, and no official revenue is public. (2) The closest comparable to a battery report is AVILOO. It sells a 3-minute SoH test to garages at GBP 35 per test (ex VAT) against a GBP 95 retail price, and has more than 550,000 tests, EUR 30M of growth funding and OEM, leasing and auction customers. Its UK partner price implies about 37% of RRP goes to AVILOO and the garage keeps the rest. (3) Public SoH check prices in Germany are EUR 49 to 149 (ADAC, TUV NORD, TUV Rheinland, AVILOO retail). Latvian guides quote EUR 30 to 80 for an OEM-tool SoH read. (4) A full-vehicle drive-through scanner (UVeye) is sold as expensive per-lane SaaS to large dealer and OEM channels. Its USD 191M raise in Jan 2025 shows the category is capital-heavy, which a Riga start-up should not copy. (5) Report businesses scale on volume and data. carVertical had EUR 75.8M revenue in 2025 at about EUR 8 to 30 per report, but it sells data, not physical inspection. (6) Pure-play data and OBD-dongle plays failed or pivoted. Verizon Hum closed on 31 Dec 2025, and Otonomo's value fell from USD 1.4B at its SPAC listing to a reported ~USD 70M at its merger with Urgently. Wrench (mobile mechanic and inspection) kept consolidating through acquisitions, with no shutdown found. Data for Latvia is thin. No public Latvian price list for EV or HV diagnostics was found, and only low-quality directory prices (EUR 25 to 45 for computer diagnostics). The honest implication is that garages and dealers will pay roughly EUR 35 to 60 net per battery report if it replaces a 90-minute OEM-tool job, but a physical full-body scanner is not needed to sell that. Conclusion: sell the battery SoH report (and triage grade) first, via a partner-style per-test price, and treat the rest of the scanner as an unproven add-on.

items.topic: asTech / Repairify (US remote scan-as-a-service): pricing
items.finding: asTech ships a pass-through OEM scan tool to collision shops and supports it remotely. Pricing is dated and conflicting across press reports; no current official price sheet was found. One 2021 article reports USD 50 per pre-scan and 50 per post-scan, with an extra USD 69.95 if a DTC is found or further diagnostics are needed (Porsche 100 and 199.95). An older report quotes USD 119 pre and 50 post for one shop. GEICO signed a standardized-pricing agreement with asTech in July 2024 for its Auto Repair Xpress shops. A mobile calibration provider complained that the GEICO-set price is under half of reasonable cost for specialty vehicles. Lesson: the buyer of the scan is often the insurer, and standardized prices squeeze the service provider. Per-transaction price is USD 50 to 120, small compared with a EUR 60 to 130 battery test.

items.topic: Repairify (asTech parent): scale and revenue
items.finding: Repairify reported 12.4M diagnostic scans, 4.9M reports and over 28,000 commercial customers in 2021, with USD 1.3B of facilitated work-order billings. items.topic: Bosch and Hella Gutmann remote diagnostics for multi-brand garages (EU)

items.topic: AVILOO B2B: closest comparable (battery SoH report sold to garages, dealers, leasing, auctions)
items.finding: AVILOO sells a 3-minute FLASH test (and a longer PREMIUM test) via a pay-per-test partner model. Through its UK partner MotorCheck the cost is GBP 35 per test ex VAT with no minimum volume, recommended retail GBP 95 (about GBP 60 margin per certificate), or unit rental GBP 35 per month on a 12-month term. The report is VIN-tied and gives SoH %, usable energy, cell voltages (min/avg/max), BMS and sensor checks, DTCs, isolation resistance and a signed TUV-certified PDF or API. It claims about 96% EV coverage. The test reads data through the OBD port, not by scanning from outside the car; it is a data-plus-model product, which supports the idea that a physical scanner is not needed for SoH. AVILOO says it has more than 550,000 tests, 30+ countries, customers including BCA, Cox Automotive, ADAC, Emil Frey, Arval, Ayvens, Hedin, and OEMs Mercedes, Volvo, Hyundai and Porsche Holding. It took about EUR 30M of growth financing in Feb 2026 (Armira Growth, Invest AG). In June 2026 it launched a free-to-buyer 1-year battery warranty (EUR 3,000 cap, individual SoH floor at 20,000 km) and a dealer dashboard called AVILOO Connect; in Sept 2026 the warranty was extended to 14 more markets (24 in total; Latvia/Baltics not named). Revenue is not disclosed. Lesson: B2B partners buy a cheap, fast, certified number, and AVILOO monetizes via per-test fees plus warranty risk and data. Its 2022 launch price at ADAC was EUR 49, rising to 99 after June 2022.

items.topic: Test-house battery checks (TUV Rheinland/Twaice, TUV NORD, DEKRA) and report format
items.finding: TUV Rheinland's Battery Quick Check (JV with Twaice, via Hella Gutmann tool) has a non-binding RRP of EUR 149; it applies a load via a diagnostic tool and wallbox for about 90 minutes (5 minutes of technician time), compares with a lab reference, and works only for specific models (about 40 models, roughly 50% market coverage by end of 2023). It argues that BMS-reported SoH is not a reliable indicator. TUV NORD's BatterieCheck costs EUR 89.90, reads battery data through the diagnostic interface (no disassembly), takes minutes and gives a report with an SoH score, an interpretation, a buy/sell recommendation and CARA-standard certification; it asks for at least 20% charge and last full charge within 14 days. Another press guide cites DEKRA or TUV Sud at just under EUR 100 net. Takeaway: in Germany a 'battery check' is a EUR 79 to 149 retail product that always starts at the OBD port or charger. A garage-facing report should be priced somewhat below that, around the AVILOO partner model.

items.topic: UVeye (drive-through vehicle scanner): business model and funding
items.finding: UVeye sells AI vehicle-scanning gates (undercarriage, body, tyres) via quote only, as a subscription or pay-per-scan. Third-party pricing sites say USD 6,000 to 7,000 per lane per month plus USD 7,000 to 12,000 site prep (one cited Forbes range of USD 3,000 to 5,500 not verified); a review cites a USD 8,500 early-removal fee, auto-renewing 2-year contracts and USD 2.50 per extra scan. A Volvo dealer case study claims USD 31 average extra parts/labour per scan and suggests at least 40 vehicles a day to make sense. GM offered dealers credits of up to USD 2,500 per month towards a UVeye subscription (2024). UVeye raised USD 191M in Jan 2025 (USD 41M equity led by Woven Capital, USD 150M debt via Trinity Capital), after a 2023 Series D valued at USD 800M to 1B; revenue is unverified (conflicting estimates). Takeaway for Riga: even the leader needs OEM and large-dealer channels and high volumes; a single-site scanner at 3,500 imports a year (about 10 per day) cannot reach the break-even volumes cited above. Marketing claims about seeing the battery are weak: an underbody scanner sees only the pack housing and cannot read cell health. The SoH report still depends on BMS or load data.

numbers.value: USD 6,000 to 7,000 per lane per month; site prep USD 7,000 to 12,000

items.topic: Failures and lessons
items.finding: Verizon Hum (OBD dongle plus subscription) was discontinued on 31 Dec 2025; analysts attribute it to built-in OEM telematics and carrier dependence. Otonomo (connected-car data marketplace) listed via SPAC at USD 1.4B in Aug 2021 and, per a secondary report, was worth about USD 70M when it merged into Urgently in Feb 2023 (all-stock, 67/33). One commentator said its data coverage did not translate into monetizable services. Reviews of Wrench/YourMechanic cite warranty and quality disputes (Trustpilot, self-selected). No evidence was found of Wrench shutting down. Lessons for us: do not sell raw data or dongles; sell a decision-ready certified output with a clear buyer; avoid being dependent on OEM data access, which Regulation 2023/1542 Art. 14 may help or not (fee and platform terms not confirmed); keep unit economics per test simple; insurers and OEMs can set the price.

items.topic: Regulation 2023/1542 Art. 14 and what it implies for the business model
items.finding: EUROBAT (Dec 2025) says Art. 14 covers SoH and expected lifetime and requires BMS to hold up-to-date SoH data from 18 Aug 2024 for EV, LMT and stationary batteries; read-only access via a standard diagnostic protocol is described in a manufacturer compliance note. A vendor (Arianee) claims Annex XIII restricts SoH data to repairers, refurbishers and end-of-life operators and authorities (not verified against the text). Whether independent operators can be charged fees, and any connected-car data platform duty, were not found. Implication: access to SoH data via OBD is becoming a legal right for independent operators, which lowers the barrier for competitors and means the moat is certified methodology, trust and distribution, not data access.

Wheelstreet.lt is a Vilnius used-EV seller founded 2025, not a Latvian source. Do not present its EUR 30-80 as the Latvian garage price level.
Repairify 'scans' are not revenue or even paid transactions of a single type, and the figures are 2021 company claims. Do not use 28,000 customers as current evidence.

The Reg. 2023/1542 Art. 14 point and the user's premise of 'independent operators read access' were not verified against the legal text. The researcher's own wording (Annex XIII restricts SoH data to repairers, from a vendor) is not verified and Annex XIII concerns the battery passport, so do not use in the pitch without reading EUR-Lex.

missed: Direct evidence on what an external scanner can see of an installed pack is thin. The strongest supporting fact is that every priced battery-health product found (AVILOO, TUV NORD, TUV Rheinland) works through the OBD port or a charger load. UVeye's own materials only cover physical damage such as leaks, cracks and corrosion. The researcher should have framed 'scanner cannot measure SoH' as an inference from absence of evidence, plus the physics of an enclosed, sealed pack.

TUV Rheinland says BMS-reported SoH is unreliable and uses a load test of about 90 min, while AVILOO and TUV NORD take minutes. So methods and accuracy differ, and a EUR 35-60 garage report price is for the quick OBD-type check, not the validated load test. No independent accuracy comparison was found, only vendor claims.
TUV NORD's report is accepted for use on sales portals and 'as evidence in court' (vendor claim). Certification and trust, not scanning hardware, are the moat in this segment.

Price anchors on the buy side: TUV NORD at EUR 89.90 retail is below TUV Rheinland at 149 and AVILOO's German retail of 79-99, so there is no single German price. A Riga price of EUR 60-130 sits at the top of the OBD-based range.
carVertical's EUR 75.8M and AVILOO's 550k tests are both self-reported; no revenue for AVILOO is public, so 'the closest comparable scales' cannot be backed by a revenue figure.

Otonomo closed its merger in Oct 2023 at an exchange ratio of 0.51756, implying roughly USD 282M for the combined equity, per a search summary (not opened). This would add nuance to the 'data business collapse' story.

findings.angle: D: Latvian and Baltic demand and competition
findings.summary: Public data on the Baltic service and inspection market is thin, and several asked-for figures were not found. Found: CSDD runs 33 technical inspection stations (63 inspection lines) and did 1,272,583 inspections in 2024; Latvia has about 13k EVs, Lithuania about 20k (Oct 2025) and Estonia about 8k (end 2024); Latvian garages are widely reported to lack EV skills, and EV-capable independents are few. The CSDD periodic inspection has no battery SoH test, and the EU Roadworthiness Package still has no confirmed SoH method. Benchmark SoH test prices are EUR 30-120 (Aviloo EUR 99 retail); the team's EUR 60-130 range sits inside that. No price found for what importers, leasers or insurers pay for inspections; no Baltic EV-diagnostics competitor price list; no CSP service-sector totals; no Estonia or Lithuania inspection-station counts; no 2025 used-EV import count. The 3,500/yr used-EV import figure was not corroborated or contradicted; the January 2025 Auto Asociacija figures are internally inconsistent. findings.angle: E: economics, legal and data issues of a diagnostic center
findings.summary: Result of ~20 searches and 10 fetches (EN, LV, DE). Caveat: the search tool returns summaries, so only fetched pages (marked "fetched") were read directly. A stationary scanner lane has NO public price anywhere: UVeye is lease-only, and the only monthly figures come from trade press and a low-quality site, all in USD for the US. Floor space and power for a lane were not found. The mobile OBD plus thermal route is well priced: Autel Ultra EV about EUR 4.4-5.5k plus renewals, FLIR E8 Pro EUR 2,799, and EV battery tests are already sold at EUR 70-150 in Germany. Law: Art. 14(2) of 2023/1542 gives read-only BMS SoH access to whoever lawfully acquired the battery and independent operators acting for them. The Data Act and Regulation 2018/858 (C-296/22) support owner-consented data access. A VIN is personal data only when the recipient can link it to a natural person (C-319/22). Latvian rules: MK 295/2017 is the state-inspection regulation, and a May 2026 draft would let accredited, procured providers do the inspection. A private diagnostic report is not a state inspection, so no CSDD licence is needed for it (my inference, not confirmed by a source). Nothing found on liability insurance pricing, Riga industrial rent in 2026, Latvian ISO 9001 prices, LATAK fees, van prices or drive-over tyre scanner prices. Critical point on what a body scanner sees of an installed battery: it is an exterior and underbody imager (damage, leaks, corrosion, tyre wear, body panels). It cannot see cells or SoH. SoH must come from the BMS/OBD or a charge/discharge test, and even the BMS figure is unreliable (arXiv 2026: correlations 0.10-0.62, 384 of 1,114 EVs gave no SoH).

items.topic: What a scanner can and cannot see of an installed battery (critical)
items.finding: Drive-through scanners (UVeye, Proov, Michelin) are optical/exterior and underbody imaging: leaks, corrosion, damage, tyre/body condition. They never see inside the pack; at most they show underbody impact damage or leaks on the pack casing. Vendor sources give no battery SoH claims; I found no source showing any scanner measures SoH. Thermal imaging: searched, no source found for assessing cell degradation from outside; the pack is in a metal housing, so a thermal image shows at most gross housing hot spots (my engineering inference, unverified). SoH from outside is only obtainable via BMS/OBD (TUV/AVILOO method) or a charge/discharge test. The BMS figure itself is questionable: an arXiv preprint (23 Mar 2026, 1,114 EVs, 5 makes, 375 days, submitted to Nature Energy, not yet peer reviewed, fetched) found real capacity differs 12-25% within every model, BMS SoH correlation with measured capacity only rho 0.10-0.62, and 384 vehicles did not expose SoH at all. A Michelin page claims one automated inspection every 3 minutes vs at least 30 minutes manual (vendor claim, no price).

items.topic: Battery Regulation Art. 14 (EU 2023/1542) access to SoH data
items.finding: Art. 14(1): from 18 Aug 2024 the BMS of EV, LMT and stationary batteries must hold up-to-date data on the parameters of state of health and expected lifetime (Annex VII). Art. 14(2) (fetched, German text via gesetze.legal): any person who lawfully acquired the battery, and independent operators acting on their behalf, get read-only, non-discriminatory access via the BMS, subject to the manufacturer's IP, for (a) offering to independent aggregators, (b) assessing residual value, remaining life and further use, (c) reuse/repurposing/remanufacturing. Consequence: the center needs the owner's authorization and a purpose within (b) or (c), i.e. residual value assessment is covered. Caveats: Annex VII is a parameter set (for EVs state of certified energy), not a single SoH percent; the delegated act with minimum values under Art. 10(5) has not been adopted (per a code repo comment, secondary); I could not confirm any 2027 date. Where the SoH reading is not shown to be accurate (arXiv study), a report claiming it needs a disclaimer. Official EUR-Lex text was not opened directly.

items.topic: EU Data Act and OBD access (vehicle data)
items.finding: Data Act (Reg. 2023/2854) applicable since 12 Sep 2025 (trade press, LKQ Europe). Users get free access to data generated by a connected vehicle and can direct it to third parties (Art. 4-5); third parties get it on FRAND terms; DMA gatekeepers are excluded as recipients (Art. 5(3) per most summaries; source conflict, verify in the text). Owner consent is the gate: the diagnostic center must have the owner's instruction, and the data is limited to what the vehicle generates, not infrastructure. Separate legal channel: CJEU C-296/22 (ATU/Carglass v Stellantis Italy, Oct 2023) held that independent repairers must have read and write access to OBD data under type-approval Reg. 2018/858, and that security measures cannot restrict it (via Taylor Wessing and others, secondary). A Commission document C(2026) 1811 on OBD/RMI and secure access is circulating in the Council (ST-7952-2026), contents not read. Gap: no post-Sept 2025 practical enforcement or Latvian-specific OEM data portal evidence found, so how easily a Riga center gets OEM data (in-vehicle server data beyond OBD) is not confirmed.

items.topic: GDPR: VIN, number plate, consent, processing agreements
items.finding: CJEU C-319/22 (Gesamtverband Autoteile-Handel v Scania, 9 Nov 2023): a VIN is not personal data by itself but becomes personal data for anyone who has reasonable means to link it to an identifiable natural-person owner. A scanning center that records the plate, VIN and the owner's contact details together, in one report, therefore processes personal data. The disclosure to independent operators by manufacturers was justified under Art. 6(1)(c) (legal obligation, Reg. 2018/858). Latvian regulator DVI (2021 decision, Latvian text, search excerpt only) treats a registration number together with make/model as potentially personal data. EDPB Guidelines 01/2020 on connected vehicles: consent is the preferred legal basis; location data high risk; only collect what is necessary (secondary summaries). ANPR/plate recognition: lawful basis would likely be Art. 6(1)(b) contract or 6(1)(f) legitimate interest with a documented balancing test (general knowledge, not sourced here); keep retention short. Roles: when the center scans for a garage that orders the report, a data processing agreement (Art. 28) is needed; the center is a controller for its own report. Specific Latvian rules on ANPR or workshop DPAs: not found.

items.topic: Latvian vehicle inspection and certification
items.finding: State technical inspection (valsts tehniskā apskate) is organised by CSDD under Cabinet Regulation No. 295 (2017) (regulation name per search summary; current wording not verified). A Ministry of Transport draft of 22 May 2026 (fetched, consultation until 5 June 2026) would let accredited providers, chosen by public procurement, do the technical inspection, with CSDD organising and supervising. Draft status not verified. A private diagnostic report on battery/body condition is not a state inspection, so I found no rule that stops a private firm issuing a non-statutory report (my inference; check with CSDD or a lawyer). Whether a private firm may call it an 'inspection' (apskate/pārbaude) or use the CSDD-style certificate layout was not checked. Accreditation: LATAK accredits inspection bodies against LVS EN ISO/IEC 17020 (Kiwa Latvia is LATAK-I-132); ISO/IEC 17020:2026 (Edition 3, March 2026) is the current version per the ISO page snippet. 17020 is voluntary for a commercial diagnostic report, but gives a trust signal and independence (Type A/B/C) rules matter, as a center that also sells repair or battery buying would fail the impartiality test as a Type A body. LATAK fees: not found.

synthesis.verdict: Split verdict. (1) The "full body scanner that scans the battery" is NOT real as a battery test. Drive-through scanners (UVeye, Mercedes/DVS-type camera arrays) see the car's skin, tyres and underside. For an installed pack they can at most show casing damage, leaks and missing shields. I found no product, vendor document or independent data showing any drive-through scanner measures state of health (SoH), capacity, cell balance or internal faults. Real SoH numbers come from the car's data port (OBD/BMS), a short loaded drive, or a charge-load test, not from imaging. (2) The business idea underneath, "a diagnostic center that sells a decision-ready electronic report to garages", is real but crowded at the SoH layer: AVILOO, DEKRA, TUV NORD, TUV Rheinland/TWAICE, TEXA, Hella Gutmann and Mahle already sell it, and Reg. 2023/1542 Art. 14 lowers the barrier for everyone. (3) Owning a scanner lane is a bad bet for a start-up: about EUR 150k purchase per lane (trade press), no Baltic reference customer, and our volume (about 10 used-EV imports a day if the uncorroborated 3,500/yr is right) is far below what lane vendors say is needed. Recommendation: do not buy a scanner. Build a small battery-first diagnostic and triage service (OBD/BMS SoH via a licensed partner method + a human or phone underbody check + our own grade and routing), sell the report to garages, importers and leasers at a price below the retail SoH tests, and use it as the lead engine for take-back, second life and recycling. Treat the scanner as a later add-on via a partner who already owns one. Main weakness of the whole idea: the SoH method is not ours, accuracy claims by vendors are unvalidated, and we have no evidence yet that Latvian garages will pay for it.
what_a_scanner_can_and_cannot_see: PHYSICALLY POSSIBLE (physics, not products): cameras see only what is visible, and many EV packs sit behind underbody plates, so a camera sees the plate, not the pack. A sealed, shielded, liquid-cooled pack hides its cells from infrared and visible light. An infrared camera reads surface temperature only and cannot see through the housing; it needs an active load and a baseline, and a parked car at ambient temperature is thermally quiet (my inference; FLIR EV safety whitepaper, vendor, undated). X-ray/CT can see through the housing and show internal geometry (misalignment, deformation, swelling) but not capacity.

SOLD BY VENDORS (marketing, not independently validated): UVeye CEO said in Aug 2023 the underbody scanner 'checks for broken EV battery cases' and battery-health sensors were still in development (Unite.ai interview, 2023-08-07; vendor claim). FreightWaves 2 Oct 2025 says thermal imaging for EV battery monitoring is 'being integrated' in the heavy-duty truck platform, availability 'expected in 2026'; no specs, no follow-up found as of 31 Oct 2026. UVeye's homepage (checked 31 Oct 2026) mentions no EV battery feature. Instavalo (Germany) says an underbody check could reveal battery damage or wrong re-installation (autohaus.de, 14 Jul 2025, vendor). Vumo snippets say it 'estimates EV battery condition' but its own product page does not mention EV batteries; its 'up to 95%' accuracy has no defined metric. Treat 'MRI for vehicles' (Hertz release wording) as marketing.

PROVEN / PLAUSIBLY SUPPORTED: underbody cameras detect leaks, missing parts, corrosion, scrapes and obvious casing damage; the Swiss HV-battery guideline (SVV, Feb 2026, official) treats casing deformation of 10 mm or more, holes or torn casing as grounds to exclude the battery without further inspection, so a flagged casing is a real triage trigger. Even this has no independent accuracy study that I found (one forum anecdote alleges a false positive led to an unneeded replacement; unverified). Hertz's own figure: more than 97% of 500,000 scanned rentals showed no billable damage (Global Fleet, 2025-08-01), and a US House Oversight letter on AI damage billing is dated 2025-08-20, which shows false-positive and dispute risk for automated verdicts.

CAN SEE (casing level): dents, punctures, scrapes, deformation of the pack housing, coolant/fluid leaks nearby, missing or loose shields and fasteners, corrosion, signs of repair or bad re-installation.

CANNOT SEE: capacity or SoH, internal resistance, cell imbalance, chemistry or cell maker, fast-charge history, internal shorts, swelling inside the housing (only X-ray), insulation resistance or water ingress (needs electrical measurement), BMS software faults.

WHAT DOES SEE INSIDE: Fraunhofer AIR full-vehicle X-ray (360 kV, tested on more than 100 private EVs, about 10 min scan and about 5 min automated evaluation) shows layer misalignment, deformation and swelling, but not SoH, has no price, no commercial availability and no announced roadworthiness use (ASNT Materials Evaluation 2026-05-01; electrive 2026-09-22). Fraunhofer XXL-CT resolves installed modules at 0.5-1 mm but is a lab facility in Furth, 'too expensive for private individuals' (Fraunhofer IIS, 2023-01-31, official). Neither fits a service-centre lane.

WHAT MEASURES SoH: OBD/BMS read plus cloud model (AVILOO Flash about 3 min; TUV NORD BatterieCheck minutes), a short loaded drive (DEKRA about 15 min: static data plus about 100 m acceleration, model-specific parameters, claimed +/-2.5% error only at 10-30 C, mean error under 9% from -10 to 40 C, vendor slide deck), or a load during AC charging (TUV Rheinland/TWAICE via Hella Gutmann, about 60-90 min). All accuracy figures are vendor claims; I found no independent validation of any of them.

WARNING ABOUT THE BMS NUMBER ITSELF: an unreviewed preprint (arXiv 2603.21592, 23 Mar 2026; 1,114 EVs, Hyundai/Kia/Genesis/Audi/VW only) found BMS-reported SoH correlates poorly with measured capacity (rho 0.10-0.62), and 384 vehicles expose no SoH at all. So even the OBD route has a quality problem; it is a preprint on five makers, not proof for all cars.

OBD for 'other data': standard OBD2 readers show few generic codes on EVs; cell voltages and insulation values need OEM or advanced tools (XENTRY, ODIS, ISTA; low-authority German workshop source). Swiss guideline lists the useful BMS reads: DTCs, SoC, cell and module voltages, module temperatures, cell-voltage difference, insulation values, SoH, pyrofuse state.

business_model_options.option: A. Battery SoH + triage report sold per test to garages, used-EV importers and dealers (recommended start)

business_model_options.price_points: Anchors: AVILOO partner cost GBP 35 vs GBP 95 retail (UK); TUV NORD EUR 89.90; TUV Rheinland EUR 149; ADAC EUR 79; Lithuanian blog EUR 50-120 and a Latvian-language broker guide EUR 30-80 for an OEM-tool read (commercial, undated). Our EUR 60-130 range is at the top of the OBD-based range. Hypothesis to test: EUR 50-90 retail, EUR 35-60 net to a garage that resells.
business_model_options.capex: Low: OBD readers or licensed boxes (about USD 1,095 per Autel EV kit; AVILOO unit rental GBP 35/month UK terms), laptop, training. No lane.

business_model_options.option: B. Intake lane: partner or rent a scanner (UVeye-type) for importers, fleets and auctions, battery casing flag only
business_model_options.who_pays: Large importers, leasers, rental fleets, auction houses; OEMs through dealer programmes.
business_model_options.price_points: Not found for Baltics. Reported per-lane USD 3,000-7,000/month (unverified); my arithmetic: a EUR 4-6k monthly lease needs roughly 30-100 paid tests at EUR 60-130 just to cover the lease, before staff, site and power.

Plus false-positive disputes, vendor failure (Proov), and the scanner adds nothing for SoH.

business_model_options.option: C. Remote report platform for service centres: one electronic file per car (SoH, DTCs, casing photos, tyres, our grade, recommended action) via portal/API
business_model_options.who_pays: Garages and service chains, possibly leasers and insurers.
business_model_options.price_points: Subscription plus per report, like DEKRA's SaaS terms (prices not published). Garages pay small sums for expert help today (EUR 385/year hotline, 2019). Likely EUR 10-30 per report on top of the test if bundled (my estimate, untested).
business_model_options.capex: Low to medium: software development, API/PDF, hosting.

demand_evidence_in_latvia_and_baltics: Fleet size: 12,991 EVs (1.6% of cars) on 1 Oct 2025 per CSDD as reported by LSM 2025-10-26 (seen only via search summary; not opened). Your 13,916 is a different date or definition: label it with its source and date. The 'nearly 10,000 registered in 2024' iFinanses figure is most likely stock, not annual registrations (LSM 2025-02-05 says just over 8,000 in stock and about 2,000 registered in the prior year).

Used-EV imports: the 3,500/yr figure is NOT corroborated or contradicted. Auto Asociacija/iFinanses (2025-04-15): used EVs were 22.9% of used cars registered in Jan 2025, +11% y/y, but the article's absolute counts are inconsistent and one month cannot be annualised. Action: pull first-registration-of-used-vehicles by fuel type from CSDD open data.

Subsidy driver: old Latvian scheme (used EV EUR 3,350/5,000/6,750) ran out Aug 2025 (LSM 2025-10-12). New EUR 40M scheme approved 21 Apr 2026, EUR 3,000-9,000 per vehicle, used EV only if max 7 years old, under 150,000 km and registered in Latvia no more than 12 months before (LSM 2026-04-21). That favours freshly imported used EVs, which is exactly the import-inspection niche. Check whether it asks for a battery test (not found).

Garage capacity gap: LSM 2025-02-05 says most garages in Latgale do not service EVs and the Latgale technical college (173 mechanic students) has no EV classes; LSM 2022-01-19 says only 'one or two' non-dealer places could repair EVs. No count of EV-capable garages exists in any source I found. This supports demand for a ready report but is qualitative.

Market statements: Transporent (SIXT franchise partner) says its own fleet batteries lost up to 15% and recommends sellers give a battery certificate; SEB Leasing says OEMs may replace below about 70-80% capacity within 8 years / 160,000 km (jauns.lv 2024-08-22; company statements, not market statistics). Auto Bassadone Riga says a battery test at a certified dealer shows remaining capacity. This is the closest thing to a demand statement from leasing and rental.
Price effect of SoH on used value: cars under 80% SoH sell about 6-12% cheaper than above 90% (EVtrader, vendor, 2025). Vendor claim, but explains why importers might pay for a certificate.

Inspection context: CSDD did 1,272,583 inspections in 2024 with 63 lines (CSDD slide deck 2025-02-26; I could not verify the PDF text, station count 31 vs 33 unresolved). Periodic inspection price EUR 34.10 from 1 Mar 2025 (LSM 2025-02-11). No EV battery SoH step in CSDD inspection found; no CSDD plan for one found.

Baltic neighbours: Lithuania about 20,000 electric cars (LSM 2025-10-12), used-EV registrations 1,046 in Oct 2025 (reidasofficial.lt, blog); Estonia 8,044 BEVs end-2024 (Transpordiamet-cited thesis) and a subsidy that ended. Regional hub would be 40-80k BEV+PHEV (researcher's rough estimate, weakly sourced).

NOT FOUND: what importers, leasers, insurers or dealers in Latvia pay for inspections; any Riga price list for EV battery diagnostics; number of garages in Latvia (CSP data); any Baltic AVILOO/DEKRA partner; any local scanner deployment. So there is no hard evidence yet that Latvian garages will pay for a diagnostic report.
legal_and_data_issues: Reg. (EU) 2023/1542 Art. 14: per the consolidated text on gesetze.legal (a legal-text mirror, NOT EUR-Lex; confirm on EUR-Lex before the pitch), the BMS must hold SoH and expected-lifetime data from 18 Aug 2024; any person who lawfully acquired the battery, expressly including independent operators, waste managers and third parties acting for them, gets non-discriminatory read access to those data via the BMS for residual-value assessment and reuse/repurposing/recycling; Art. 14(3) requires a BMS software reset function. Caveats: the right belongs to the battery owner or whoever acts for them, so a diagnostic centre needs an owner mandate; manufacturer IP is protected; no standard technical access method is defined. One earlier research pass wrongly described access as 'legitimate interest' under implementing acts; that wording belongs to the Annex XIII battery passport, not Art. 14. Battery passport for EV batteries reportedly from Feb 2027 (Codibly, vendor).

Vehicle OBD/RMI access: Reg. (EU) 2018/858 Art. 61 gives independent operators OBD and repair information. Delegated Reg. (EU) 2026/699 (adopted 23 Mar 2026, in force 23 Jun 2026; Noerr summary) lets OEMs use certificates and tokens at secure gateways, with API duties phased 23 Sep 2026, 23 Dec 2026, 23 Jun 2027 and 23 Jun 2028, and adds battery diagnostics and repair info (Annex X 2.5.12/2.5.13). Security-relevant access needs SERMI certification (valid 5 years). I read this via a law-firm summary, not the primary text. Practical battery-data access is not settled.

EU Data Act: applicable since 12 Sep 2025; connected-vehicle design duty from 12 Sep 2026. Users can authorise third parties, but most OEMs use 'extended vehicle' servers, so it does not give a garage a live OBD read.

Personal data (my assessment, not from the research): VIN plus owner plus location of repair is personal data under GDPR; reports sent to garages need owner consent, a data processing agreement and retention rules. Needs a lawyer.

Liability and trust: a wrong SoH or a false 'damaged casing' flag can change a car's price or trigger an unneeded pack replacement. The Hertz/UVeye billing dispute and US House Oversight letter (2025-08-20) show the reputational risk. Reports need disclaimers, a human review step for adverse findings, and insurance.

Certification: buyers trust TUV, DEKRA and AVILOO labels. DEKRA SaaS requires trained authorised personnel with compliance checks; AVILOO reports are TUV-certified; TUV NORD and TEXA reference CARA certification. Using their method means accepting their licence terms; our own method would have no accepted standing.
Safety: working on high-voltage vehicles requires HV training (Swiss guideline: HV1/HV2 for non-live work). X-ray (if ever used) brings radiation licensing; not relevant to the minimum version.

Roadworthiness: the EU Roadworthiness Package (2025/0097(COD)) is in trilogue (Council approach 5 Dec 2025; EP mandate 21 May 2026, 369-126-84 per search summary; 2nd trilogue debrief 20 Oct 2026; no deal found). Parliament adds test items for battery-electric/hybrid vehicles, but no confirmed SoH capacity test and no uniform EU method. Latvia/CSDD has no battery SoH rule. This is a possible tailwind or a threat (inspection bodies could add SoH), not yet a requirement.
UNECE GTR 22 (adopted 2022-03-09) will require on-board state-of-certified-energy monitors on new BEVs; it helps future comparability but not used imports on the road today.
fit_with_our_battery_business: Lead generation: every diagnostic is a contact with a car owner, importer or garage at the moment the battery state is known. Cars with low SoH or damaged casings are the earliest signal of future pack take-back. This is the strongest fit, and it needs no scanner.

Pack triage: our existing health test (EUR 60-130, Riga) is the same product as the OBD SoH report. The new angle is packaging it as a standard electronic file for garages (grade, damage flags, DTCs, recommended action) and routing outcomes: keep driving, repair module, replace pack, second life, recycle. Swiss guideline thresholds (deformation 10 mm or more, holes, heat above 60 C) can seed our own exclusion rules.

Second-life sourcing: the diagnostic gives early access to packs and to history (SoH, cell spread, insulation, DTCs) that raise the value of what we later buy. Art. 14(2) explicitly covers reuse and repurposing assessment, which supports the use case, with owner mandate.

Used-EV import channel: importers are the one concentrated buyer group (subsidy rule favours recently registered used imports). Selling them a certificate per car plus a take-back option for packs that fail is a natural bundle.
Recycling: damaged-casing flags identify cars where a pack may be unsafe or uneconomic to repair, relevant to take-back logistics and safety.
Conflict-of-interest warning: if we both test and buy the pack, we need transparent rules and probably an independent-looking certificate (partner method) to be trusted.
Distraction cost: a scanner lane would tie up capital and attention away from pack take-back and second life, where our edge is.
synthesis.minimum_version_we_could_start_with: "A paid pilot of about 30-50 cars in 6-8 weeks, no scanner. (1) Method: get a licensed OBD SoH method from a partner (ask AVILOO, DEKRA, TUV NORD and TEXA for Baltic partner terms) or use our current test, and be explicit about which it is. (2) Visual check: a human underbody and tyre checklist with 6-10 phone photos taken on a ramp or lift at a partner garage, covering pack casing, shields, leaks, tyres and any warning lights. (3) Report: one PDF plus a simple link or JSON file per car with SoH, BMS/DTC findings, photos, our triage grade (green/yellow/red), and 'what to fix or do next' for the garage, signed with owner consent. (4) Customers: 2-3 used-EV importers and 3-5 independent garages in Riga; offer the first reports at a discount in exchange for feedback and a price test (EUR 50, 70, 90). (5) Track: reports sold, price accepted, how often the report changed a decision, and how many packs became take-back leads. Add a scanner only if an operator offers pay-per-scan access with a battery casing flag and enough volume."
rough_costs: Scanner purchase: about EUR 150,000 per camera-array scanner (Mercedes dealer scanner, leinetal24.de 2026-10-16, trade press, single source); DVS EUR 200-250k (older, undated). Scanner lease: ProovStation EUR 4-6k/month (stale, vendor now restructured); UVeye USD 3-7k per lane per month (third-party, unverified, conflicting). Site works and staffing not found. My arithmetic: a EUR 4-6k/month lease equals roughly 30-100 paid tests per month at EUR 60-130 just to cover the lease.

OBD SoH route: AVILOO UK partner GBP 35 per test (no minimum) or GBP 35/month unit rental (vendor, 31 Oct 2026); EU/Latvian terms not found. Autel EV diagnostics upgrade kit USD 1,095 (vendor). Hella mega macs X about EUR 2,490 plus VAT (comparison site, undated). Bosch ESI about EUR 500-1,500/year (estimate). TEXA needs IDC6 CAR plus TEXPACK subscription (price not found). Tesla Toolbox 3: USD 75/day, USD 150/month, USD 700/year (InsideEVs, Nov 2025).

Our own pilot (my estimate, not sourced): tool licences or readers EUR 1-5k, HV safety training, insurance, a part-time technician, report template and simple portal development. Total likely in the low tens of thousands of EUR for a pilot; to be priced by the team, not a researched figure.

Revenue side (anchors): a garage-net price of EUR 35-60 per report (hypothesis based on AVILOO GBP 35 cost / GBP 95 retail and EUR 79-149 retail tests) times about 10 cars a day would be about EUR 90-160k per year of gross revenue at full capacity; I treat this as an illustration, because the 3,500/yr import figure is uncorroborated and a single lane would not capture all of it.
Regulatory/legal: counsel for GDPR and owner-mandate templates; SERMI certification only if we need security-relevant OEM access (cost not found).
Not found: Latvian service-centre pricing for EV diagnostics, AVILOO/DEKRA Baltic licence fees, UVeye real quote, Fraunhofer AIR price.
risks: Product risk: the headline idea ('scanner sees the battery') fails in front of any technical judge; pitching it as stated invites a fast rejection. Reframe around the report and triage.

Competition and substitution: AVILOO (EUR 30M raised Feb 2026, 24-country warranty), DEKRA, TUV and the tool makers already sell SoH; garages can buy a Hella or Autel tool for roughly EUR 2.5-5k; Art. 14 gives competitors the same access rights.
Accuracy and trust: no independent validation of any commercial SoH method; BMS-reported SoH is unreliable (preprint); our report could be wrong and damage reputation.
Demand is unproven: no Latvian price list, no count of EV-capable garages, no evidence of what importers or leasers pay; the 3,500 import figure is unverified.
Small market: Latvia about 13k EVs; EV-capable independents are few; Baltic total only interesting as a regional hub; subsidy scheme can change.
Capex trap: scanner lanes need volume, OEM or large-dealer channels and long contracts; vendor risk (ProovStation insolvency, UVeye debt-funded growth); false-positive disputes.
Data access: OEM gateways and tokens (Delegated Reg. 2026/699 phase-in through 2028), no standard technical interface for Art. 14, owner mandate required; some makes will not expose SoH.
Conflict of interest between testing and buying packs; trust and legal exposure if grading steers sellers to us.
Timing: team is on a hackathon clock (pitch Sun 1 Nov 2026, 12:30 Riga); a half-researched scanner story is a weak point under questions.

Source quality: several key figures are vendor claims or undated third-party estimates; EUR 30-80 Latvian-language price is from a Lithuanian used-EV seller (commercially interested), not a Latvian price list.
next_steps: Day 1-2 (before the pitch): reframe the idea as 'battery-first diagnostic and triage report; scanner optional later'. Use only sourced numbers; drop the unverified UVeye valuation (USD 800M), the USD 3-5.5k/month lane price, Puspakom, and the 'AVILOO 3 min = ADAC EUR 79' pairing (ADAC lists about 30 min at its office). Say Art. 14 access needs owner mandate and cite EUR 14 text only after checking EUR-Lex.

Day 1-3: read Art. 14 and Annex VII/XIII on EUR-Lex (official text) and Delegated Reg. 2026/699 primary text; pull CSDD open data on first registrations of used vehicles by fuel type to replace or confirm 3,500/yr and 13,916 EVs (label dates and sources).

Day 2-5: phone/email AVILOO (Vienna) and MotorCheck for EU/Baltic partner terms, DEKRA and TUV NORD/Rheinland for licence or SaaS terms, TEXA and Hella for Baltic distributors and pay-per-use certificate prices. Ask UVeye's new UK/EU GM and the Mercedes scanner operator for a real quote and a pay-per-scan option, plus whether they flag battery casing damage.

Day 3-8: interview 8-10 buyers in Riga: 3 used-EV importers, 3 independent garages, 1-2 leasers or rental firms (e.g. SEB Leasing, Transporent), 1 insurer, CSDD. Ask what they pay today, what they would pay per report, what format they want, and who owns the decision.
Day 5-10: design the report (one page: SoH, key BMS values, damage flags, photos, grade, next action) and test it with 3 garages for comprehension: can they tell what to fix in under 2 minutes?
Day 7-12: test 5-10 cars with two methods if possible (our current test and a partner OBD test) and compare, to see how much results differ; record it as an internal accuracy check, not a validation.

Day 10-14: decide go/no-go on the pilot using three thresholds set in advance: number of buyers willing to pre-commit, accepted price, and share of tests that create a take-back lead. Defer any scanner decision until a partner offers pay-per-scan access.
questions_that_need_a_human: What would AVILOO, DEKRA, TUV NORD or TEXA charge us per test or licence in Latvia, and do they allow us to resell under our name or only as a white-label? Do they already have a Baltic partner?

Will an OEM allow a garage with owner mandate to read SoH in practice (which makes, via which tool or gateway), and what does each OEM charge independent operators? Ask Tesla, VW group, Hyundai/Kia importers in Latvia.

What do Latvian used-EV importers, leasers, insurers and dealers pay today for a battery check or inspection, and would they pay for a certificate per car? (No Latvian price list exists in public sources.)

How many used EVs were first-registered in Latvia in 2025 and 2026 year to date (CSDD open data or a direct request)? Does the new EUR 40M subsidy scheme (approved 21 Apr 2026) require a battery test?
Does CSDD or the Ministry of Transport plan an EV battery check at periodic inspection, and would CSDD stations act as partners for a test point?
What is a real UVeye/Mercedes-type scanner quote, pay-per-scan price, minimum volume and contract term, and do they flag EV battery casing damage on European cars?

Legal: does a report that grades a battery and a business that also buys the pack need specific consumer-law or competition treatment in Latvia? What GDPR basis and consent wording should we use for VIN-linked reports?
Insurance: what professional liability cover is needed if a report influences a car's price or a repair decision?
Which HV safety qualification do our staff need for the pilot, and does a workshop partner already hold it?
